Class GameBlockRenderer

Namespace
OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering
Assembly
OnixRuntime.dll

Allows you to render game blocks, this is a little more involved of a process than calling a magical render block function, but the results are pretty good. You get almost every block and their hardcoded behavior handled for you, occlusion if you set it up. It's still a lot less involved than implementing all of this yourself!

Properties

Cache

This is what the GameBlockRenderer goes to everytime it needs a block. This lets you cheat by changing the cache yourself to manipulate the rendering. Very notably, UseOccluder needs to be properly setup in order to work. The cache contains a region of 20x20x20 blocks, which is meant to be a subchunk and two blocks around it. Going outside the cache usually will lead to air being returned.

public GameBlockRendererCache Cache { get; }

CurrentVisualShape

You should probably use SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) instead of setting this yourself. The current visual shape of the block being rendered. You should just set CurrentBlock and CurrentPosition then explicitly set CurrentShapeSet to false. This will make the game retrieve the proper shape on its own, which will likely be better than what you will come up with. You can even collect it after it is done rendering the block too!

IsRenderingExtra

This is to tell the renderer that it is rendering the extra block, or the block at the layer 1. This is for waterlogged blocks or foliage with snow in it. You would use GetExtraBlock(BlockPos) to get the extra block, you'd SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) and after that, set this to true. Remember to not render it if it's air.

UseOccluder

The occluder is what allows the faces that aren't visible to not be rendered. This does not do camera based culling, only at the face level, seeing if a block is hiding that face. This is very useful but requires a little more work to work properly. You need to make sure the Cache is properly filled up/reset with a position that can be accessed in the cache. The cache contains a region of 20x20x20 blocks, which is meant to be a subchunk and two blocks around it. Going outside the cache usually will lead to air being returned and no culling/occlusion.

public bool UseOccluder { get; set; }

Parameters

renderPosition BlockPos

This will be where the block will be rendered but the world block doesn't have to match the blockToRender. The issue is that if you do UseOccluder, this will use the Cache to determine if it should be occluded or not. Now if the block you're trying to do isn't actually in the world, but you still want to occlude, you could manually fill up the cache.

blockToRender Block

The block you want to render.

blockFace BlockFace

The face of the block you're trying to render. Just remember, not everything is a full block and this won't give the best result on non-full blocks.

forcedVariant int

This is to force a specific variant of a block, you should probably not touch that, the game half hardcodes values for those.

Returns

RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block)

If you're looking for opacity or tinting, look at RenderBlockTinted(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block, ColorF). This function does require setup before it is used. You can get SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) to do most of it for you. You should try to batch blocks into a single mesh whenever possible. You should re-use that mesh as generating those meshes can be quite slow. You will probably want to SetMaterialCustom(string, bool) use a custom material like "terrain_alpha" or "terrain_blend" or "terrain_opaque" (note that "terrain_blend" decided to not work on 1.21.40 specifically...) Now to use this, you will need a GameMeshBuilder that has a session started. Remember that this function can only render with Quad. For testing, you should likely use applyReverseOriginOffsetIf3D and add -32 or something to the height of PostTransformOffset. This will let you see the results so you know you're doing something right. Once you're ready to get serious, you can put it to false and offset it by the invert of the first block on the x and y (assuming you're rendering a group of blocks of course.) This will then let you offset it where you want without much precision loss using PushTransformation(TransformationMatrix, bool) before rendering the mesh. Once you rendered every block you want, call Build(bool, bool) to get the mesh out of it. Note: You should never render an air block. You'll get the update block otherwise. Don't hesitate to ask for help if you do need some. You can also look at the examples below.

public void RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder meshBuilder, BlockPos renderPosition, Block blockToRender)

Parameters

meshBuilder GameMeshBuilder

A GameMeshBuilder That has started.

renderPosition BlockPos

The position at which you want to render that block, this will render it at that position in the world, but also take things like rotation for that position. (How a few blocks like grass or sand rotates depending on its world position.) It doesn't have to match where the block actually is or actually exist in the world. Note that if you DO use UseOccluder you will absolutely want to trick the Cache if the position does not match to ensure the desired result.

blockToRender Block

The block that you actually do want to render.

Examples

This example shows how to render a block at a specific position. Specifically, mirror a block that's in the world. Taking the player's targeted block and rendering it two blocks above.

 private void OnWorldRender(RendererWorld gfx, float delta) {
    // Check if we are even looking at a block.
    if (Onix.LocalPlayer is { Raycast: { Type: RaycastResultType.Block } }) {
        // Get the block we're targeting's position in the world.
        BlockPos blockPos = Onix.LocalPlayer.Raycast.BlockPosition;
        // Get is as a block.
        Block block = Onix.Region!.GetBlock(blockPos);
        // This lets us support waterlogging / snow with foliage inside.
        Block extraBlock = Onix.Region!.GetExtraBlock(blockPos);
        // Get the coordinates of the second block from the one we're targeting.
        BlockPos desiredRenderPosition = blockPos.Up.Up;
        // Never render an air block guys!
        if (!block.IsAir()) {
            // Start a new mesh builder session with quads.
            using (var session = gfx.NewMeshBuilderSession(MeshBuilderPrimitiveType.Quad, ColorF.White, TexturePath.TerrainAtlas)) {
                // Usually for more complex movement, you'd probably want to use a transformation matrix, especially that you would have saved the mesh.
                // For now, this will offset the vertices further, causing them to be where we want them.
                // And since we're rendering a block that is actually in the world, it means we won't have to mess with the cache.
                session.Builder.PostTransformOffset = session.Builder.PostTransformOffset + new Vec3(desiredRenderPosition - blockPos);
                // Get our wonderful block renderer.
                var blockRenderer = gfx.BlockRenderer;
                // Let it do the basic configuring for us, no need to go into the weeds here.
                blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(blockPos, block);
                // We don't want to hide any faces in this case, plus setting up the occluder is a bit more efforts.
                // Since we're not using an occluder, no real need to reset the cache.
                blockRenderer.UseOccluder = false;
                // If we want biome tinting to work, we have to reset the cache. You may not care about that so that's why it's manual.
                blockRenderer.ResetBiomeCache(blockPos);

                // Add the block onto our mesh builder session.
                // For one block it's fine to not use an occluder but for larger volumes, you should consider setting it up.
                blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, blockPos, block);

                // Render the second layer if any. Remember, don't render air. Don't do it guys.
                if (!extraBlock.IsAir()) {
                    // Setup this new block at our new position.
                    blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(blockPos, extraBlock);
                    // We're rendering an extra block right now, not the main block. Let it know.
                    blockRenderer.IsRenderingExtra = true;
                    // And render that one too!
                    blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, blockPos, extraBlock);
                }

                // For lighting, it usually puts UVs from the light texture into the UV1 slot of the vertices.
                // Since we can't provide it, we make sure it's not rendering from whatever was last bound there.
                session.Builder.DisableUv1();
            } // Now, if we had anything to render, when that } calls Dispose() it should render our block with the material we picked.
        }

    }
}

This example shows how to render a single block that is not actually in the world at a specific position.

 private void OnWorldRender(RendererWorld gfx, float delta) {

    // Easy example: Render a specific block that is not really in the world.
    // Gets the water and fence block we want to render. (the ?? is because the fence changed its name at some point, so this handles both cases)
    Block oakFenceBlock = (Onix.World!.BlockRegistry.GetBlock("oak_fence", 0) ?? Onix.World.BlockRegistry.GetBlock("fence"))!;
    Block extraBlockWater = Onix.World.BlockRegistry.GetBlock("water")!;
    // Get the coordinates of where we want to render, in my case it'll be at 5, 5, 5.
    BlockPos fakeBlockRenderPosition = BlockPos.FromString("5 5 5");
    // Start a new mesh builder session with quads.
    using (var session = gfx.NewMeshBuilderSession(MeshBuilderPrimitiveType.Quad, ColorF.White, TexturePath.TerrainAtlas)) {
        // Get our wonderful block renderer.
        var blockRenderer = gfx.BlockRenderer;

        // We'll need to cheat the cache to get the result we want, first we have to reset it.
        // In this case, we could probably get away with not resetting it, but because of the water
        // We have to reset it and lie, otherwise it becomes a flat plane.
        blockRenderer.ResetCache(fakeBlockRenderPosition);
        // If we want biome tinting to work, we have to reset the cache. You may not care about that so that's why it's manual.
        blockRenderer.ResetBiomeCache(fakeBlockRenderPosition);
        // This is our actual block we want to render, we'll put it in the cache for good measure
        blockRenderer.Cache.SetBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, oakFenceBlock);
        // I also want this fence to be waterlogged, so let's set that too.
        blockRenderer.Cache.SetExtraBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, extraBlockWater);


        // Let it do the basic configuring for us, no need to go into the weeds here.
        // We give it the position we tampered with in the cache.
        blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, oakFenceBlock);
        // We don't want to hide any faces in this case, plus setting up the occluder is a bit more efforts.
        blockRenderer.UseOccluder = false;

        // Add the block onto our mesh builder session.
        // For one block it's fine to not use an occluder but for larger volumes, you should consider setting it up.
        blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, fakeBlockRenderPosition, oakFenceBlock);

        // Render the second layer, in this case we know we have one so no checks.
        // Setup this new block at our new position.
        blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, extraBlockWater);
        // We're rendering an extra block right now, not the main block. Let it know.
        blockRenderer.IsRenderingExtra = true;
        // And render that one too!
        blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, fakeBlockRenderPosition, extraBlockWater);

        // For lighting, it usually puts UVs from the light texture into the UV1 slot of the vertices.
        // Since we can't provide it, we make sure it's not rendering from whatever was last bound there.
        session.Builder.DisableUv1();
    } // Now, if we had anything to render, when that } calls Dispose() it should render our block with the material we picked.
}

This example shows how to render more than one block, in this case part of a chunk. You can adapt it or learn from it to build your own larger meshes but it should be a good starting point.

 private GameMesh? _subChunkMesh = null;
 private void OnWorldRender(RendererWorld gfx, float delta) {
    // Only generate a mesh when we don't have one already.
    if (_subChunkMesh is null) {
        var mb = gfx.MeshBuilder;
        var blockRenderer = gfx.BlockRenderer;


        // We start our new session here, note that I'm not applying the reverse origin, since we're going to render it at the origin.
        // Well at least at the mesh level.
        mb.New(ColorF.White, MeshBuilderPrimitiveType.Quad, false);

        // Get our coordinates for what we want to pick up.
        // We'll take two sub chunks from height 0. We'll pick the chunkToGrab chunk data.
        // Of course, you can do less or more, you have to split it up for the cache though.
        int subChunksToInclude = 2;
        ChunkPos chunkToGrab = new(0, 0);
        BlockPos chunkStartPos = new(chunkToGrab.X * 16, 0, chunkToGrab.Y * 16);

        // We're going to offset our first block to be at 0,0, 0 when the mesh is built, which is the invert of our first block's position.
        mb.PostTransformOffset = new Vec3(-chunkStartPos);

        for (int currentSubChunk = 0; currentSubChunk < subChunksToInclude; currentSubChunk++) {
            // Reset our cache to this subchunk. I'll also surround with air so the sides are visible.
            // The bottom and top will also be surrounded, but not of every subchunk, only the first and last.
            bool shouldSurroundTopAndBottom = currentSubChunk == 0 || currentSubChunk == (subChunksToInclude - 1);
            blockRenderer.ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(chunkStartPos.WithY(chunkStartPos.Y + currentSubChunk * 16), true, shouldSurroundTopAndBottom);
            // If we want biome tinting to work, we have to reset the cache. You may not care about that so that's why it's manual.
            blockRenderer.ResetBiomeCache(chunkStartPos.WithY(chunkStartPos.Y + currentSubChunk * 16));
            for (int x = 0; x < 16; x++) {
                for (int y = 0; y < 16; y++) {
                    for (int z = 0; z < 16; z++) {
                        // This gets our coordinates from our for loops into a BlockPos
                        BlockPos currentBlockPos = new(chunkStartPos.X + x, chunkStartPos.Y + y + currentSubChunk * 16, chunkStartPos.Z + z);
                        Block blockAtPos = Onix.Region!.GetBlock(currentBlockPos);
                        // Don't render air guys!
                        if (blockAtPos.IsAir()) continue;

                        // Setup our block as before, no need for anything fancy.
                        blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(currentBlockPos, blockAtPos);
                        // Tell it to occlude faces we can't see, this doesn't do anything with the camera, just at the mesh level.
                        // Still, that's very good and since we've set up the cache, it should be able to detect what it needs.
                        blockRenderer.UseOccluder = true;

                        // And send it!
                        blockRenderer.RenderBlock(mb, currentBlockPos, blockAtPos);

                        // And now, to support the second layer, waterlogging, etc.
                        Block extraBlockAtPos = Onix.Region!.GetExtraBlock(currentBlockPos);
                        if (!extraBlockAtPos.IsAir()) { // Just don't render air!
                            // Set that block up.
                            blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(currentBlockPos, extraBlockAtPos);
                            // We're rendering an extra block right now, not the main block. Let it know.
                            blockRenderer.IsRenderingExtra = true;
                            // Send that one too, great that one block is done and added to our mesh.
                            blockRenderer.RenderBlock(mb, currentBlockPos, extraBlockAtPos);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        // For lighting, it usually puts UVs from the light texture into the UV1 slot of the vertices.
        // Since we can't provide it, we make sure it's not rendering from whatever was last bound there.
        // This has to be done before we build/render the mesh.
        session.Builder.DisableUv1();

        // Okay, we've just finished adding all those blocks, that probably took some time but now time to convert it to a mesh.
        // That way, we don't have to do all that work again. Make sure to put immediate to false.
        _subChunkMesh = mb.Build(false);
    }

    if (_subChunkMesh is not null) {
        // Now, to render it. It's quite tricky to find a material, but this seems to give decent results.
        // Pretty well with almost every block, doesn't support blending or tinted glass very well though.
        // This is why we have render layers exposed now, so you can try to do different things, good luck.
        gfx.SetMaterialParameters(new GameMaterialParameters() {
             AlphaTest = true,
             Uv = true,
             Gradient = true,
         });

        // Now we have to position it, remembered how we made sure to render it at 0,0,0?
        // Now we have to move it not only back into view but where we actually want to render it.
        // Whatever position we do give, will represent the block in the bottom corner with the smallest coordinates.
        // I'll render mine at 16, 10, 16. You can pick any coordinates in 3d, sub-coordinates. Rotate it, scale it, have fun!
        TransformationMatrix transformation = TransformationMatrix.TranslateWorldPosition(16, 10, 16);
        using (_ = gfx.PushTransformation(transformation)) {
            // Finally, while that transformation is applied, let's render our mesh. 
            // Don't forget to give it the terrain texture atlas!
            // And that's done, you should see a copy of your chunk where you rendered it.
            // The inside should be hollow if you set up your cache and enabled UseOccluder.
            // To reflect the changes of course, you'd have to rebuild the mesh.
            gfx.RenderMesh(_subChunkMesh, ColorF.White, TexturePath.TerrainAtlas);
        }
    }
}

RenderBlockTinted(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block, ColorF)

Sorry, I don't really want to put every example here again, please see RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block) for examples. This function does require setup before it is used. You can get SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) to do most of it for you. You should try to batch blocks into a single mesh whenever possible. You should re-use that mesh as generating those meshes can be quite slow. You will probably want to SetMaterialCustom(string, bool) use a custom material like "terrain_alpha" or "terrain_blend" or "terrain_opaque" (note that "terrain_blend" decided to not work on 1.21.40 specifically...) Now to use this, you will need a GameMeshBuilder that has a session started. Remember that this function can only render with Quad. For testing, you should likely use applyReverseOriginOffsetIf3D and add -32 or something to the height of PostTransformOffset. This will let you see the results so you know you're doing something right. Once you're ready to get serious, you can put it to false and offset it by the invert of the first block on the x and y (assuming you're rendering a group of blocks of course.) This will then let you offset it where you want without much precision loss using PushTransformation(TransformationMatrix, bool) before rendering the mesh. Once you rendered every block you want, call Build(bool, bool) to get the mesh out of it. Note: You should never render an air block. You'll get the update block otherwise. Don't hesitate to ask for help if you do need some. You can also look at the examples in RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block).

public void RenderBlockTinted(GameMeshBuilder meshBuilder, BlockPos renderPosition, Block blockToRender, ColorF tint)

Parameters

meshBuilder GameMeshBuilder

A GameMeshBuilder That has started.

renderPosition BlockPos

The position at which you want to render that block, this will render it at that position in the world, but also take things like rotation for that position. (How a few blocks like grass or sand rotates depending on its world position.) It doesn't have to match where the block actually is or actually exist in the world. Note that if you DO use UseOccluder you will absolutely want to trick the Cache if the position does not match to ensure the desired result.

blockToRender Block

The block that you actually do want to render.

tint ColorF

The tint to use when rendering. Note that for opacity, you'd give a white color with the desired opacity.

ResetBiomeCache(BlockPos)

This resets the biome cache for this subchunk, you should call if you want biome tinting to apply. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is.

public void ResetBiomeCache(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition)

Parameters

worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos

The starting position of your sub chunk.

ResetCache(BlockPos)

This resets the cache to an empty state, you should call this before doing anything with the cache. This will do -2 to the position you add to it, so you should just give it the start of your subchunk. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is. When rendering a subchunk, if you want the sides to render too, you should call ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(BlockPos, bool, bool) instead to surround it in air at the same time.

public void ResetCache(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition)

Parameters

worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos

The starting position of your sub chunk.

ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(BlockPos, bool, bool)

This resets the cache to an empty state, you should call this before doing anything with the cache. This will do -2 to the position you add to it, so you should just give it the start of your subchunk. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is. When rendering a subchunk, if you want the sides to render too, this is the function for it!

public void ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition, bool sides = true, bool topAndBottom = true)

Parameters

worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos

The starting position of your sub chunk.

sides bool

True if you want the sides to be surrounded by air.

topAndBottom bool

True if you want the top and bottom faces to be surrounded

SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType)

Sets up a lot of renderer parameters for you. Note that you should make your changes after calling this function if the defaults don't satisfy you. Note that this does not touch UseOccluder. You are responsible for managing this bit yourself as it requires more flexibility than this simple function can provide.

public void SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos pos, Block block, GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType lightingType = BlockLightingType.BakedWithAmbientOcclusion)

Parameters

pos BlockPos

The position of the block in the world.

block Block

The block to set it up for.

lightingType GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType

The kind of lighting you want.

Remarks

Here is what this function does for you.

CurrentShapeSet = false;
CurrentBlock = block;
CurrentPosition = pos;
RenderingLayer = block.RawRenderLayer;
IsRenderingExtra = false;
IsRenderingGui = false;
UseNormals = false;
LightingType = lightingType;
CurrentScale = 1.0f;
